section.title: If the Lord Had Not Been on Our Side
section.sectionRationale: A Song of Ascents of David, fifth in the pilgrim collection Psalms 120 to 134, placed in Book V of the Psalter, Psalms 107 to 150. Where earlier ascents cried out in distress and rejoiced at arrival, this psalm turns back to remember how close Israel came to being lost, and why she still stands.
section.thesis: Israel's survival against overwhelming enemies rests entirely on the LORD's help, not on human strength, so His people are taught to declare that their help is in the name of the LORD who made heaven and earth, a truth fulfilled in Christ who delivers His people from every foe.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the conditional peril if the LORD had not been on Israel's side, verses 1 to 2, the overwhelming danger pictured as beasts and floods, verses 3 to 5, praise for the LORD's deliverance, verses 6 to 7, and the closing declaration of trust, verse 8.

units.label: If the LORD had not been on our side

verses.text: If the LORD had not been on our side, let Israel now declare,
if the LORD had not been on our side when men attacked us,

units.label: The raging waters would have swept us away

verses.text: when their anger flared against us, then they would have swallowed us alive,
then the floods would have engulfed us, then the torrent would have overwhelmed us,
then the raging waters would have swept us away.
Blessed be the LORD, who has not given us as prey to their teeth.
We have escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowler; the net is torn, and we have slipped away.

units.label: Our help is in the name of the LORD

verses.text: Our {{ezer|help}} is in the name of the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth.

ezer.gloss: Help, aid, one who comes alongside in a time of need. The same root names the memorial stone Ebenezer, 'stone of help', 1 Samuel 7:12, marking the LORD's rescue of His people.

basic.context: This Song of Ascents, attributed to David, is a corporate confession sung by pilgrims recalling how close Israel came to destruction, and how entirely her survival depended on the LORD rather than on her own strength.
basic.hermeneutics: It describes a specific remembered deliverance from overwhelming enemies, and it prescribes as an abiding pattern the humble confession that God's people owe every rescue to the LORD's help alone.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalm closes on the word ezer, help, the same root behind Ebenezer, the stone of help. Israel's whole song is built on the confession that her help, past and future, is found only in the name of the LORD.
basic.typology: The bird escaping the fowler's broken snare anticipates the greater deliverance Christ accomplishes for His people from the snare of sin and death, and the LORD as Maker of heaven and earth anticipates Christ, through whom all things were made and by whom His people are kept.
basic.christ: Paul takes up this psalm's logic directly, 'If God is for us, who can be against us?', Romans 8:31, and Hebrews 13:6 echoes its confession, 'The Lord is my helper, I will not be afraid.' Christ is the decisive proof that God is for His people, and He has broken the power of sin and death that once held them fast.
basic.god: The LORD is the one on whom Israel's survival depended entirely. He restrains the fury of her enemies, breaks the snare set to destroy her, and is Himself her help because He is the Maker of heaven and earth, sovereign over every threatening power.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 8:31-32 applies this psalm's confidence to the church. Hebrews 13:6 echoes its declaration that the Lord is a helper who casts out fear. Hebrews 2:14-15 shows Christ breaking the power of him who held people in bondage through fear of death.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's confession that Israel's rescue depended wholly on the LORD's help is answered decisively in Christ, in whom God is for His people, breaking the power of sin and death and becoming Himself their everlasting help.

context.literary:
Psalm 124 is a single sentence stretched across eight verses, and the stretching is the point. Verses 1 and 2 open with an 'if' that is left hanging, and the missing half arrives only in verse 3 with 'then.' The reader is made to stand at the edge of the disaster for two full verses before seeing what would have happened. The leader's cue, 'let Israel now declare,' sits inside the unfinished sentence, so that the whole congregation is called to finish it aloud.

The poem has three movements. Verses 1 to 5 are a hypothetical past: what would have followed if the LORD had not been for Israel. Verses 6 and 7 are the actual past: He has not given us up, and we are free. Verse 8 is the present and the future in one line: our help is in the name of the LORD. The grammar steps from 'would have' to 'has' to 'is,' and each step brings the singer closer to safety.

Two pictures of danger are laid on each other. The first is a beast, 'swallowed alive,' 'prey to their teeth.' The second is water, 'floods,' 'torrent,' 'raging waters.' The third is a hunter's trap, 'the snare of the fowler.' The images run from the monster's mouth to the flood to the net, a descent in cunning, and the rescue comes in the quietest picture, a bird slipping away from a broken snare. The psalm moves from huge threats to a small bird to show that the same God who restrains the flood can also free a single life.

The word 'then' appears three times in verses 3 to 5, and each repetition adds a layer of disaster. The relief is similarly built in repetition: 'Blessed be the LORD,' then 'the net is torn,' then 'we have slipped away.' The psalm ends with a short confession that is sung rather than argued, 'Our help is in the name of the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth.' It ties together the fifteen songs by echoing Psalm 121:2, and it is echoed again in Psalm 134:3.
context.historical:
The psalm names no battle, but its three images match the dangers Israel knew. Hostile nations were a constant, 'when men attacked us,' verse 2. The Old Testament often pictures an invading army as a flood. Isaiah compares the king of Assyria to 'the mighty floodwaters of the Euphrates' that would overflow Judah 'reaching up to the neck,' Isaiah 8:7 to 8. In a land of dry valleys, a wadi that is empty at noon can become a torrent in an afternoon storm, and a traveller caught in it has no time to escape. The word for 'torrent' in verse 4 is the Hebrew word for such a stream bed.

The fowler's snare was a household reality. Hunters spread nets and traps for birds, and Proverbs 6:5 pictures a bird freed from the fowler's snare. Psalm 91:3 also promises that the LORD will deliver 'from the snare of the fowler.' To say that Israel escaped 'like a bird' is to say that the escape was beyond the bird's own power, since a bird caught in a net does not break it.

The psalm's heading attributes it to David, and David's reign supplied many occasions when Israel was nearly overwhelmed, from the Philistine wars to Absalom's revolt. Yet the language is general, and later generations would have sung it after other escapes. The post-exilic community had its own reasons for gratitude. Nehemiah's builders were threatened by Sanballat and his allies, and Nehemiah says the enemies' plot was frustrated by God, Nehemiah 4:15. The psalm is built to be sung on any such occasion, and the call 'let Israel now declare' makes it a public liturgy rather than a private memory. It also appears in the same collection as Psalm 129:1 to 2, which opens with the same call and says that Israel has been persecuted many times from her youth, 'but they have not prevailed against me.'
context.canonical:
Psalm 124 stands between Psalm 123, where the people wait under contempt, and Psalm 125, where they are secure as Mount Zion. Its place in the sequence is a memory, a look back to being rescued that gives strength for the next waiting. The Songs of Ascents often alternate between present difficulty and recalled help. This psalm is the major recollection.

The call 'let Israel now declare' comes again in Psalm 129:1 and in Psalm 118:2, where Israel is told to say 'His loving devotion endures forever.' These are liturgical rubrics, and they show that such psalms were sung responsively. The confession 'The LORD is on my side; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?' of Psalm 118:6 is a nearly exact parallel to verse 1 and the pilgrim's sense of the LORD on Israel's side.

The water imagery recurs across the canon as a picture of threat and rescue. Psalm 18:16 to 17 says that the LORD 'drew me out of deep waters.' Psalm 69:1 to 2 prays, 'Save me, O God, for the waters are up to my neck.' Isaiah 43:2 promises, 'When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and when you go through the rivers, they will not overwhelm you.' Psalm 46:1 to 3 tells of a world in upheaval in which God is 'an ever-present help in times of trouble.' The Exodus is the foundation of this pattern, where 'the LORD saved Israel from the hand of the Egyptians,' Exodus 14:30. Samuel's stone Ebenezer, with its 'Thus far the LORD has helped us,' 1 Samuel 7:12, is the same confession in a memorial. In the New Testament, Paul answers verse 1 with 'If God is for us, who can be against us?' Romans 8:31, and the writer to the Hebrews quotes the confidence of Psalm 118:6, 'The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid,' Hebrews 13:6.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author wanted Israel to say the one sentence that every deliverance proves: it was the LORD. The opening is not 'If we had been stronger' or 'If we had been cleverer,' but 'If the LORD had not been on our side.' By stating the danger first and at length, he made sure the singers would not forget how bad it was. Gratitude that skips the danger is cheap. The psalm asks the people to feel what they were saved from.

He also meant them to see that survival is a matter of the LORD's character and not of their record. 'Blessed be the LORD, who has not given us as prey to their teeth,' verse 6, makes the LORD the active party who refused to hand them over. Israel is not a lucky nation. It is a kept one.

Third, the last verse is meant to settle the people for the future. The confession turns the memory into a rule: if the LORD was our help then, He is our help now. The pilgrim going up to Jerusalem is not to rely on his own strength to survive the next threat. The psalm gives the whole assembly the words of faith and the creed of their dependence, 'Our help is in the name of the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth.' It is a statement meant to be sung until it is true in the heart as well as on the tongue.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm tells what the LORD did. It does not promise that every threat will be turned aside and no believer will be 'swept away.' Christians have been swallowed by persecution, floods have taken faithful people, and the psalm itself comes from a nation that was later carried into exile. To read verses 1 to 5 as a guarantee that nothing bad will ever happen to those who trust God would be to turn a testimony into a contract.

The pattern the psalm sets for believers is to remember and to declare. Each deliverance, small or large, is to be traced to the LORD and spoken of with thanks. The final verse is a standing confession and may be used in any season, whether the person is at the edge of the flood or safely on the bank. It is also a corrective to self-reliance. Paul takes the confidence of the psalm and asks, 'If God is for us, who can be against us?' Romans 8:31, but he sets it beside a list of sufferings and then insists that nothing 'will be able to separate us from the love of God,' Romans 8:38 to 39. The confidence is about the final safety of the person in God's love, and not about the absence of trouble in this life.

debates.question: Is the 'if the LORD had not been on our side' language a memory of one specific crisis or a general liturgical confession?

views.label: A specific historical deliverance
views.case: The vivid, escalating images of being swallowed alive, engulfed by floods, and caught in a snare suggest a concrete, remembered crisis that Israel narrowly survived.

views.label: A generalized liturgical confession
views.case: The absence of named enemies or events fits a psalm composed for repeated corporate use, fitted to any of Israel's many close escapes rather than one single episode.

debates.bearing: Either way the psalm teaches the same abiding truth, that every rescue, past and future, belongs entirely to the LORD's help and not to human strength.

debates.question: What are the 'floods' and 'raging waters' of verses 4 and 5?

views.label: A figure for the hostile nations
views.case: Verse 2 speaks of 'men' who attacked, and Isaiah 8:7 to 8 explicitly compares the Assyrian army to floodwaters that overrun Judah. On this reading the water is a metaphor for the enemy's advance, and the single story is told in three pictures.

views.label: The waters of chaos and death
views.case: In the Psalms water often stands for the powers that threaten life itself, Psalm 69:1 to 2 and Psalm 93:3 to 4, which sets the LORD 'above the roar of many waters.' On this reading the psalm reaches beyond human enemies to the forces of death and disorder that only the Creator controls.

debates.bearing: The final line, which names the LORD as 'Maker of heaven and earth,' supports both readings, because the one who made the world rules the waters and the nations alike. The psalm is useful against any threat that is large enough to feel like a flood.

debates.question: Why are the enemies not named, and does that make the psalm timeless?

views.label: The lack of names makes the psalm reusable
views.case: Because it names no enemy, the congregation of any generation can sing it of its own danger, which is how the later church has used it.

views.label: The lack of names hides a historical event we cannot recover
views.case: The heading and the specificity of the images suggest an actual event whose details have been lost, and the text should not be flattened into a general principle.

debates.bearing: Interpreters should not claim to know the event. They may use the psalm as Israel did, applying the confession to whatever threat is at hand.

study.originalLanguages:
The conditional that opens the psalm is built with lule, a Hebrew particle meaning 'if not,' 'had it not been.' It begins both verse 1 and verse 2, in the form 'if not the LORD, who was for us.' The phrase 'on our side' is the Hebrew shehayah lanu, literally 'who was to us' or 'who was for us.' The small preposition carries the whole sense, that the LORD has been for Israel. Paul's 'If God is for us,' Romans 8:31, speaks the same relation in Greek. The covenant name is the first thing in the psalm after the 'if,' and it returns in verses 2, 6 and 8, four times in all, so that the personal name of God frames the poem like four posts.

Verse 1 says 'let Israel now declare,' yomar na Yisrael, with the small particle na, 'please' or 'now.' It is a polite summons, the way a leader calls a congregation to speak. The same formula opens Psalm 129:1, and Psalm 118:2 has a similar call. The subject is 'Israel,' the whole people, so that the confession is corporate. In verse 3 the enemy 'swallowed' us alive uses the verb bala, to swallow, with the word 'alive,' chayim. The pairing recalls the fate of Korah's company, when 'the earth opens its mouth and swallows them,' and they 'go down alive into Sheol,' Numbers 16:30. Proverbs 1:12 uses the same pair of words, 'let us swallow them alive like Sheol.' The enemies are pictured as the grave itself, opening to receive Israel.

Verses 4 and 5 use the Hebrew word nefesh, which the BSB leaves untranslated by saying the torrent would have 'overwhelmed us.' The Hebrew speaks of the waters passing over 'our soul.' Nefesh means life, the whole person, and also the throat or neck, the place where a drowning person feels the water rise. Psalm 69:1 says, 'the waters are up to my neck,' with the same word. The word appears again in verse 7, 'we have escaped like a bird,' where the bird is the nefesh, so the psalm opens with the soul beneath the flood and ends with the soul in the air. The two phrases for rushing water, mayim and nachlah, one the general word and the other the wadi, are placed in parallel to show that the disaster is entire.

Verse 6 uses teref for 'prey,' from the word for what a beast tears. Its sense is flesh that has been ripped apart, and it has the same root as the verb in Genesis 37:33, where Jacob says Joseph has been torn by a wild animal. The psalm's picture is of Israel as an animal's kill, which makes the line 'has not given us' a refusal by God to hand His people over. The verb is natan, 'give,' and God is the only one with the power to give or withhold.

In verse 7 the snare is described as broken, shabar, a word that usually means to shatter, and the verb for escape, malat, is repeated. The 'fowler,' yaqush, appears in Psalm 91:3 as well. The bird is freed by God's act on the net. The final noun in verse 8 is ezer, 'help,' the word used in Genesis 2:18 of the woman as a helper corresponding to the man, and used often of God as help, as in Psalm 121:1 to 2 and Exodus 18:4. The root also appears in the name of the stone of help, Ebenezer, 1 Samuel 7:12. To place one's help 'in the name of the LORD' is to rely on His revealed character, and Proverbs 18:10 calls that name 'a strong tower' that the righteous run to and are safe.

typology.type: The snare broken and the bird freed, Psalm 124:7
typology.fulfillment: Israel escaped like a bird from a net that had been broken. Paul uses the same picture for the spiritual captives of the devil, who may 'come to their senses and escape the snare of the devil, who has taken them captive to his will,' 2 Timothy 2:26. The way the net is broken is shown in Hebrews 2:14 to 15, where Christ shares our flesh and blood so that through His death He may destroy him who holds the power of death and free those held in slavery by the fear of it. The type is correct in picturing a rescue that the captive could not accomplish. It falls short because the psalm's escape was from a human enemy and a danger in time, while Christ's is from sin and death for ever.

typology.type: The floods that would have swept us away, Psalm 124:4 to 5
typology.fulfillment: The waters that threaten to overwhelm are a recurring biblical picture of danger and death. Jesus is the one who rules them. When the disciples cried, 'Teacher, don't You care that we are perishing?' He 'rebuked the wind and the sea,' and there was a great calm, Mark 4:38 to 39. When Peter began to sink and cried 'Lord, save me!' Jesus 'reached out His hand and took hold of Peter,' Matthew 14:30 to 31. The Maker of heaven and earth of verse 8 walks among His people with the authority to still the water. The type falls short in that the psalm's flood is a figure of human enemies, whereas Christ also meets the flood of judgment, which He passes through on behalf of His people.

typology.type: The prey not given up, Psalm 124:6
typology.fulfillment: The people praise the LORD that He 'has not given us as prey to their teeth.' The New Testament shows the cost of that refusal. The Father 'did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all,' Romans 8:32. The Son was handed over so that His people would not be. Jesus described Himself as a sign like Jonah, who spent three days in the belly of the great fish, Matthew 12:40, a hint that the Son of Man would go into the place of death and come out. The correspondence is that the people were spared because another was given. The type falls short in that the psalm does not say who paid, and the gospel supplies it.

The final confession echoes Samuel's Ebenezer, the 'stone of help,' set up with 'Thus far the LORD has helped us,' 1 Samuel 7:12. The memorial stone looks back, and the psalm looks forward as well, with 'Our help is in the name of the LORD.' In Christ the help is a person who has come. Hebrews says that because He suffered, 'He is able to help those who are being tempted,' Hebrews 2:18, and invites believers to approach the throne of grace 'to receive mercy and find grace to help us in our time of need,' Hebrews 4:16. The type falls short because a stone commemorates past help, while Christ is present and living help.

study.christ:
Psalm 124 leads to Christ most plainly through Paul's use of its logic. After describing the sufferings and the hope of the believer, Paul asks, 'If God is for us, who can be against us?' Romans 8:31, and the question is the psalm's first verse turned into a rhetorical challenge. Paul then gives the proof that the psalm could not give: God 'did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all,' Romans 8:32. The psalm says 'Blessed be the LORD, who has not given us as prey.' The gospel tells how that was possible. The people were not given over because the Son was.

The psalm also points to Christ through its pictures of danger. The torrent that would have overwhelmed us is more than a political threat. The waters of death are what Christ entered. Psalm 69:1 to 2, a psalm the New Testament repeatedly connects with Jesus, cries, 'the waters are up to my neck,' and 'the flood engulfs me.' Hebrews 2:14 to 15 explains that He shared our flesh and blood so that through death He might destroy the one who holds the power of death and free those who were slaves all their lives through fear of it. What the psalm sees in the net torn and the bird slipping away, Hebrews sees in an empty grave. In the same way, Jonah's three days in the fish, which Jesus took as a sign of His own burial, Matthew 12:40, show the Son passing through the waters and coming out.

In the Gospels the Maker of heaven and earth is seen at work over the waters. Jesus 'rebuked the wind and the sea,' and 'the wind died down, and it was perfectly calm,' Mark 4:39. The disciples' question afterward, 'Who then is this?' is the question of Psalm 124:8 answered in a person, since the One who is Maker of heaven and earth is the One they have in the boat. Peter's cry on the water, 'Lord, save me!' is the cry of the psalm, and the reply is the hand of Jesus, Matthew 14:30 to 31.

Finally, the psalm's last confidence, 'Our help is in the name of the LORD,' is carried in the New Testament by the name of Jesus. Peter says that 'there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved,' Acts 4:12. The name that is a strong tower, Proverbs 18:10, is now spoken as Jesus. Believers may say with Hebrews, 'The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid,' Hebrews 13:6.

A caution is in order. The psalm does not mention a Messiah, and its original subject is Israel's rescue from human enemies. The link to Christ is by the New Testament's own use of its themes: God for us, the net broken, the one given up in our place, and the help that is a person. It would be forced to claim that the fowler is Satan in every line, or the bird is the believer in every detail, but the pattern holds.
study.god:
The psalm gives God the first and last word. It begins with His name and ends with His name, and everything between is a description of what He did. The first thing it shows is that He takes sides. 'If the LORD had not been on our side' is a statement of covenant commitment. God has bound Himself to Israel, and He has not remained neutral in her troubles. He is not like a distant spectator who watches the flood from above. The God of the covenant is in the water with His people, as Isaiah 43:2 promises, 'When you pass through the waters, I will be with you.'

He is sovereign over every threat. The psalm brings three enemies together, the beast, the flood and the hunter, and sets one God over all of them. Psalm 29:10 says, 'The LORD sits enthroned over the flood,' and Psalm 93:3 to 4 says that above the roar of many waters, 'the LORD on high is majestic.' The God of Psalm 124 is the one who is higher than the water. That is why verse 8 ends with creation: the God who made heaven and earth is able to restrain what threatens within them.

He is the One who restrains the wicked. The enemies in the psalm are angry and their anger flares, verse 3, but their fury is limited. They would have swallowed Israel but did not. That does not mean God approves of what they do. It means that He holds the leash.

He is a God of rescue, not of mere preservation. The bird is not simply kept from the trap. The trap is broken and the bird flies out. His salvation is positive, a release into freedom.

He is also a God who is worthy of blessing for what He has done. 'Blessed be the LORD,' verse 6, is praise built on a specific act. The psalm teaches that praise should be rooted in remembered facts. The people do not praise a vague goodness, they praise the One who did not give them up.

For worship, the psalm teaches humility and confidence together. Humility, because the people say that without Him they would have been lost, and confidence, because the same God is their help now. The proper response is to bless His name, to tell the story of rescue to each generation, and to confess that every escape is His doing. The name that He has revealed is a refuge, and the psalm invites every threatened person to run to it.

crossReferences.note: The previous pilgrim psalm ends its opening with 'My help comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth.' Psalm 124:8 repeats it almost word for word. The same confession stands at the start of the journey as a hope and at the end of the rescue as a testimony, which turns a promise into a lived experience.

'The LORD is on my side; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?' This is the individual form of the psalm's first verse. Both texts rest the whole of security on the LORD being on the side of His people, and both are quoted in the New Testament, Hebrews 13:6 and Romans 8:31.

When Korah rebelled, the earth opened its mouth and swallowed him and his company, and they went down alive into Sheol. The psalm's 'swallowed alive' draws on the image of the earth swallowing people. It shows how complete Israel's ruin would have been had the LORD not intervened.

The Lord will bring the mighty floodwaters of the Euphrates, the king of Assyria, over Judah, reaching up to the neck. The prophet uses water as the picture of an invading army, which supports reading the psalm's floods as the hostile nations that came against Israel.

The singer cries that the waters are up to his neck, that he has sunk in the miry depths where there is no footing. It is the experience that Psalm 124 imagines and escapes. Together they show that Israel used water as a regular figure for mortal danger.

The LORD will deliver 'from the snare of the fowler.' The same phrase appears in Psalm 124:7, and the two psalms interpret each other. One promises deliverance, and the other testifies that the promise was kept.

The LORD sits enthroned over the flood and is enthroned as King forever. This is the theology behind Psalm 124. The waters are real and dangerous, but they are under a throne, and the one who sits there is on Israel's side.

Samuel set up a stone and called it Ebenezer, saying, 'Thus far the LORD has helped us.' The root of 'help' in the stone's name is the same as the word for help in Psalm 124:8. Both mark a place where Israel stopped to say that the rescue was the LORD's.

Paul asks, 'If God is for us, who can be against us?' and answers with the cross: God did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all. It is the psalm's first verse sung in the light of Calvary, with the explanation of how God was on our side.

Christ shared our flesh and blood so that through death He would destroy the one who holds the power of death and free those enslaved by fear of it. The broken snare of Psalm 124:7 becomes a broken tyranny, and the bird's escape becomes the release of people from the fear of death.

A violent storm swamps the boat, and Jesus rebukes the wind and sea until it is perfectly calm. The Maker of heaven and earth who is named in Psalm 124:8 is shown to rule the waters in person, which answers the psalm's question of who stands between God's people and the flood.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story is one of people threatened and God rescuing. In the beginning God set limits on the waters, Genesis 1:9, and then the waters returned as a judgment in the flood of Noah's day. From Egypt, where the sea became a wall and then closed on Pharaoh's army, to the wilderness and the land, Israel's existence rests on God's rescue. Psalm 124 is the song that distills that history: the people exist because the LORD was on their side.

The psalm also helps explain why Israel could sing in the middle of danger. The pilgrims travelling to Jerusalem moved through a world of snares. They remembered the Red Sea, the wilderness, the Philistines and the exile. Each memory said the same thing. When the net was spread, God tore it. That is the confidence which carries them through the next day's journey.

But the story does not end with Israel's close calls. The prophets made clear that the flood of judgment would one day fall on Jerusalem itself, and Babylon came like water over the land. The psalm is therefore not a promise that the nation would never fall. It asks for a deeper rescue, from sin and from death. That is where Christ enters, the one on whom the flood of God's judgment fell and who, in rising, tore the net. Romans 8 states it, 'If God is for us, who can be against us?' and that is the same sentence as the psalm's opening, now made into a truth that cannot be shaken by exile or by death.

The church continues the pilgrim's song. Believers still meet the beast, the flood and the snare, and they still say, 'Our help is in the name of the LORD.' The story's end is the day when every threat is gone. In the new creation 'the sea was no more,' Revelation 21:1, and the waters that stood for chaos and death no longer rise. God's people stand on the bank, the net is torn for good, and the Maker of heaven and earth makes all things new, Revelation 21:5.

sermon.title: Three Songs of Faith
sermon.why: Begg treats Psalms 123 to 125 together, showing how this psalm's remembered deliverance grounds Israel's ongoing confidence that her help is in the name of the LORD.

quiz.q: According to verses 1 to 2, what does Israel declare would have happened without the LORD?

options.text: Enemies would have overwhelmed and destroyed them.
options.note: The whole psalm hinges on this conditional confession of total dependence on the LORD.

options.text: They would have simply lost a minor battle.
options.note: The imagery that follows is far graver than a minor loss.

options.text: Nothing would have changed either way.
options.note: The psalm insists everything hinged on the LORD being on their side.

options.text: They would have been slightly delayed in their journey.
options.note: This trivializes the psalm's picture of near annihilation.

quiz.q: What images does the psalm use in verses 3 to 5 to describe the danger Israel faced?

options.text: Being swallowed alive and swept away by raging floodwaters.
options.note: These vivid images of predators and floods picture total, overwhelming danger.

options.text: A gentle rain that caused minor inconvenience.
options.note: The text describes overwhelming, life-threatening danger, not mild weather.

options.text: A slow decline in prosperity over many years.
options.note: The danger pictured is sudden and violent, not a gradual decline.

options.text: A single arrow shot from a distance.
options.note: The imagery is far more sweeping than a single weapon, involving flood and beast together.

quiz.q: What does verse 7 compare Israel's escape to?

options.text: A bird escaping from a torn snare set by a fowler.
options.note: This is the exact image the psalm uses for their narrow, complete escape.

options.text: A soldier winning a duel.
options.note: The image is of escape from a trap, not of combat victory.

options.text: A ship reaching a safe harbor.
options.note: The psalm's imagery is a snare and a bird, not a ship.

options.text: A tree surviving a storm.
options.note: Close in theme to survival, but the specific image given is the broken snare and escaped bird.

quiz.q: Where does the psalm say Israel's help is found, according to verse 8?

options.text: In the name of the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth.
options.note: This is the psalm's climactic declaration of trust.

options.text: In the strength of her own armies.
options.note: The whole psalm denies that human strength secured the deliverance.

options.text: In alliances with neighboring nations.
options.note: No alliance is mentioned; the confession is exclusively about the LORD.

options.text: In the wisdom of her leaders.
options.note: Wise leadership is not credited here; the LORD alone is named as the source of help.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament pick up this psalm's confidence that the LORD was on Israel's side?

options.text: Paul asks, 'If God is for us, who can be against us?', grounding the church's confidence in the same truth.
options.note: Romans 8:31 directly echoes the psalm's logic and applies it to believers in Christ.

options.text: It rejects the psalm's confidence as no longer relevant.
options.note: The New Testament affirms and deepens this confidence rather than rejecting it.

options.text: It applies the psalm only to end-times armies, not to believers now.
options.note: Paul applies it to ordinary Christian assurance in the present, not merely a future battle.

options.text: It uses the psalm to warn believers against ever trusting God's help.
options.note: This misreads the New Testament's clear encouragement to trust in God's help through Christ.

questions: The psalm insists Israel's survival depended entirely on the LORD, not her own strength. Where are you tempted to credit your own strength for a deliverance that was really God's doing?
The danger is pictured as being swallowed alive and swept away, total and overwhelming. Have you known a moment of danger so real that only God's help explains your survival?
The bird escapes a torn snare, free and unencumbered. What snares of sin, fear, or circumstance has Christ broken for you, and do you live as freely as that image suggests?
The psalm ends by naming the LORD as Maker of heaven and earth, the ultimate ground for trusting Him. How does remembering God's power over all creation shape your prayers this week?
Paul takes up this psalm's very logic in Romans 8:31. How does knowing God is decisively for you in Christ change the way you face opposition or fear right now?

translationNotes.note: The repeated conditional, 'if the LORD had not been on our side,' functions as a call-and-response refrain, likely sung antiphonally by pilgrims ascending to Jerusalem.
Flood and torrent language draws on ancient Near Eastern imagery of chaotic waters as a symbol of overwhelming danger, echoing the Red Sea deliverance in Exodus 15.
Help, ezer, is the same root behind Ebenezer, the stone of help set up in 1 Samuel 7:12 to commemorate the LORD's rescue of Israel.
